# Apollo 11 radio reference

The live dialogue follows the concise call-and-response style of NASA's
[Apollo 11 Lunar Surface Journal landing transcript](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/alsj/a11/a11.landing.html).
Descent calls remain operational. Relief follows a successful landing.
Columbia stands by instead of asking casual questions during the approach.
The back-room exchange is adapted for this teaching model. Live numbers are
the simulator's metres and metres/second, not the historical mission's feet.
The simulator does not claim to reproduce the flight timeline or its telemetry.

`eagle-landed.mp3` is Neil Armstrong's actual landing announcement, from NASA
Goddard's [Sounds of the Space Age](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/sound/index.html):
[original AIFF](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/lunar/a11landing.aiff).
It plays only after a safe landing in the Flight Deck model, never for a
crash or the hardware bench's unclassified surface contact. It is an archival
quotation at a simulation milestone, not a recording of the simulated run.

The complete 3.589-second original was converted from 22,255 Hz mono AIFF
to 24 kHz mono, 96 kbps MP3, with a 1.7 dB attenuation to preserve peak
headroom. It was not voice-cloned, pitch-shifted or time-stretched.

Other lines use browser speech at natural pitch. Automatic voice selection
uses recognised English male voice names, preferring US voices. The speech
API does not expose a gender field, so ambiguous defaults are not selected.
You can choose an installed male voice explicitly. If none is recognised,
live calls appear as captions; the NASA recording remains available.
Delivery and emotion in synthesised lines remain limited by installed voices.

NASA is the source of the historical audio. Its
[media guidelines](https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/)
permit educational and informational use, including simulations and web
pages. No NASA endorsement is implied. Preserve this attribution with the clip.
